The cross-city gap scales with building height and built density, which reduce radiative loss to the sky.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI is strongest in low-density, sprawling cities with high sky view factors, this mechanism is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If reducing sky view factor (e.g., adding height) does not increase the nocturnal gap, the mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural areas with equally low sky view factors (e.g., forests) do not exhibit comparable nighttime warmth, the mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"At night, surface cooling depends on longwave radiative loss to the sky. In dense urban canyons, the sky view factor is low, so emitted longwave radiation is intercepted by opposing walls and re-absorbed, trapping heat.
